# CorX Labs — complete site content

Source: https://corx-labs.com/
Last updated: 2026-08-20
Licence of described models: Apache 2.0

===============================================================================
SUMMARY
===============================================================================

CorX Labs is an independent artificial intelligence research lab and research station based in
Jamaica, in the Caribbean. Its foundational models are built from the ground up: the architecture,
the tokenizer, the data pipeline and the training loop are all written in house, from random
weights. Where a model builds on an existing open base instead — as CorX3.8-27B does — the lab
states that plainly rather than presenting it as from scratch.

Slogan: "Architecting the future." Positioning: "from the ground up."
Founder: Nathan, a solo developer and independent AI researcher from Jamaica.
Contact: lkk89002@gmail.com
Website: https://corx-labs.com/
Models: CorX1.5 (language model, from scratch) — https://huggingface.co/Sigmandndnns/CorX1.5-160M
        TriStream-SVS (singing voice synthesis, in training) — https://huggingface.co/Sigmandndnns/TriStream-SVS-300M
        CorX3.8-27B (27B Jamaican Patois LLM, fine-tuned from Qwen3.8-27B) — https://huggingface.co/Sigmandndnns/CorX3.8-27B

===============================================================================
CORX1.5 — MODEL CARD
===============================================================================

CorX1.5 is an open-source language model with approximately 158 million parameters (157.8M), built
entirely from scratch by a single developer. Architecture, tokenizer, pretraining pipeline and
fine-tuning were all written and trained solo, on a single GPU, from the ground up. It is not a
fine-tune of an existing base model.

Hugging Face repository: Sigmandndnns/CorX1.5-160M
Developer: Nathan
Origin: Jamaica
Licence: Apache 2.0
Task: text generation
Status: actively trained; new data added on an ongoing basis

## Architecture

A custom decoder-only transformer, not copied from an existing model family.

- Positional encoding: RoPE — relative position information that extrapolates cleanly across the
  context window.
- Feed-forward: SwiGLU — gated activation, better quality per parameter than a plain MLP.
- Normalisation: RMSNorm — cheaper and more stable than LayerNorm at this scale.
- Role embeddings: a learned signal marking every token as user, assistant or raw text, so the
  model always knows whose turn it is. Most models infer this only from special tokens.
- Loss masking: assistant-only. The model is trained to predict only the tokens it should generate,
  not the user's side of the conversation.
- Parameters: 157.8M
- Layers: 10
- Context length: 1,024 tokens
- Vocabulary: 32,768-token custom BPE, trained for this model rather than reused

## Training pipeline

1. Pretraining — approximately 3 billion tokens across 25 open datasets spanning code, math,
   reasoning, conversation and general web text, with a held-out validation split and early
   stopping to catch overfitting.
2. Distillation — fine-tuned on responses generated by a larger teacher model (Qwen2.5-Instruct),
   with automated quality filtering that keeps only well-formatted, non-repetitive,
   correctly-verified answers.
3. Reasoning training — trained to show step-by-step work inside <think>...</think> blocks before
   answering, including verified worked arithmetic and debugging exercises containing a known,
   injected bug that the answer can be checked against.
4. Ongoing additions — new topics and targeted fixes are added continuously as gaps turn up in
   testing. Updated checkpoints are pushed to the Hugging Face repository; its commit history is the
   source of truth for what is current.

## What CorX1.5 is good at

- Holding a consistent identity and conversational style
- Short, direct answers to greetings and common everyday questions
- Declining requests it genuinely cannot fulfil — no internet access, no memory between chats, no
  tool access — instead of fabricating an answer
- Small worked arithmetic, shown step by step
- Recognising and explaining common Python bugs in a structured format

## What CorX1.5 is not

CorX1.5 was trained on a small fraction of the data used by comparable open models. Models in a
similar parameter range from major labs are typically trained on trillions of tokens; CorX1.5 was
trained on billions. It should not be relied on for:

- Broad factual knowledge or general reasoning outside its training patterns
- Complex or multi-step mathematics beyond basic arithmetic
- Production or safety-critical use of any kind

This is an independent research and learning project, not a competitor to frontier or lab-scale
models. It is shared in that spirit — small, transparent, and built to understand every part of how
it works.

## Safety

CorX1.5 includes a hardcoded response layer for messages indicating self-harm or crisis, which
returns a fixed set of crisis resources rather than a generated response. This is implemented in
code, not left to the model's judgment.

## Usage

CorX1.5 uses a custom architecture and is NOT compatible with AutoModel.from_pretrained() out of
the box. Load it with the model definition included in the repository (modeling_corx.py or the
provided inference script) alongside the checkpoint and tokenizer files.

    git lfs install
    git clone https://huggingface.co/Sigmandndnns/CorX1.5-160M
    cd CorX1.5-160M
    python inference.py

## Licence

Apache 2.0. Use, modification and redistribution are permitted, including commercially, provided
attribution and the licence notice are kept.

===============================================================================
TRISTREAM-SVS — MODEL CARD
===============================================================================

TriStream-SVS is a 321.8M parameter singing voice synthesis model built entirely from scratch by
CorX Labs in Jamaica. Hugging Face repository: Sigmandndnns/TriStream-SVS-300M.
STATUS: ACTIVELY IN TRAINING. No stable release checkpoint, no published benchmark scores.

## The core idea

Human voice production factors naturally into three components:
- The glottal source: vibration of the vocal folds, the raw periodic pulse train that becomes
  perceived pitch.
- The vocal-tract filter: resonant shaping by the throat, mouth cavity and tongue position. This is
  what makes a voice sound like a specific individual, and a given vowel sound like that vowel
  regardless of who produces it.
- Turbulent noise: breath, fricative consonants and non-tonal texture — the airy quality of a
  breathy delivery, the hiss of an "s".

Rather than hoping a neural network discovers this structure implicitly through training, TriStream
builds it directly into the architecture as a hard constraint.

## Building blocks

1. Source stream — 3 transformer layers. Receives ONLY a log-scaled F0 pitch contour and a binary
   voiced/unvoiced flag. It never receives the mel spectrogram, the singer embedding, or any
   timbre-carrying signal. It is architecturally incapable of representing who is singing. This
   makes the disentanglement structural rather than merely encouraged — there is no pathway through
   which timbre could reach it.
2. Filter stream — 5 transformer layers, the deepest, cross-attending to the lyric encoder.
   Receives the mel spectrogram, a singer identity embedding and an emotion/technique embedding.
   The ONLY stream that carries identity information.
3. Residual stream — 2 transformer layers. Breath noise, fricative consonants, articulation texture.
4. Lyric / phoneme encoder — 4 transformer layers, processed independently, conditioning the Filter
   stream and the Fusion Trunk by cross-attention. Keeps "what should be sung" separate from "how it
   should sound".
5. Late fusion trunk — 8 transformer layers with cross-attention to the lyric encoder. The single
   point where pitch, timbre and texture are permitted to interact. Placed as late as possible.
6. Adversarial singer head — a classifier on the trunk output trained to identify the singer, whose
   gradient passes through a gradient reversal layer. As the classifier improves, the trunk is
   pushed the opposite way, degrading its own identifiability. Domain-adversarial training used
   specifically as an ANTI-MEMORISATION mechanism.
7. Speaker encoder — a separate convolutional network for zero-shot voice cloning. Dilated
   convolutions for a wide receptive field, squeeze-excitation blocks for channel weighting, and
   attentive statistics pooling (weighted mean and standard deviation) to collapse a variable-length
   clip into a fixed-size embedding. Trained contrastively, so closeness in the embedding space
   corresponds to sounding like the same person.
8. Duration predictor — frames per phoneme, predicted in log space because note durations are
   heavily skewed.
9. Pitch predictor — separately predicts base pitch, a "scoop" component (sliding into a pitch
   rather than hitting it instantly, one of the clearest tells separating human singing from robotic
   synthesis), and vibrato depth and rate, ramped in over roughly a quarter-second. Because they are
   separate, they remain independently adjustable after generation.
10. Beat alignment — beat tracking on a supplied backing track, with SOFT quantisation and an
    adjustable swing parameter, because perfectly quantised timing is a reliable tell of synthetic
    vocals.
11. Flow-matching decoder — 5 layers using rectified flow matching. Predicts a direct velocity field
    from noise toward the target mel spectrogram instead of reversing a 100+ step diffusion process,
    giving full-quality generation in roughly 32 sampling steps.

## Two modes, one model

Editing is the NATIVE training objective: random contiguous spans of real audio are masked and the
model reconstructs them from surrounding context plus lyrics. "Regenerate this phrase with different
lyrics" is the literal task it was trained on, not an inference trick added afterwards. Generation
mode reuses the same components but starts from a fully masked target.

## Training methodology

- Singer-disjoint validation: held-out singers chosen by a stable hash and excluded at data-loading
  time, so every validation score is measured against voices never seen in training. Stricter than a
  random split, which can leak the same singer into both sets.
- Crash-resilient autonomous checkpointing: pushes to a Hugging Face repo on validation improvement
  and on a rolling interval; resumes from the latest checkpoint including full optimiser state after
  any interruption. Hardened against real data-loader and Hub connectivity failures.
- Data curation: dry, isolated vocals only. Instrumental bleed, heavy reverb and mixed-track audio
  are excluded because they corrupt the mel reconstruction target. Large-scale speech data for
  vocal-tract mechanics and phonetic coverage, plus smaller verified singing corpora for pitch,
  technique and phrasing. Every dataset is probed and verified before inclusion.
- Anti-overfitting: waveform augmentation (pitch shift, time stretch, gain), SpecAugment-style
  frequency and time masking, mixup within batches, early stopping on the singer-disjoint score, and
  preserving the best checkpoint by validation score rather than the most recent.

## Specifications

Total parameters: 321.8M. Custom transformer, source-filter factored. RoPE positional encoding.
RMSNorm. SwiGLU feed-forward. Scaled dot-product attention with cross-attention conditioning.
Rectified flow matching, ~32 sampling steps. 24 kHz sample rate (architecture supports 44.1 kHz).
100 mel bands (scales to 128). Zero-shot speaker conditioning. Singer-disjoint validation.
bf16 mixed precision.

## Limits

- NOT a stable release. No frozen checkpoint; behaviour changes between checkpoints.
- NOT benchmarked. No published objective scores, no formal listening tests. Validation loss is the
  only tracked signal, and loss is not the same as sounding good.
- NOT full-band. Output is 24 kHz with 100 mel bands today; 44.1 kHz is a future configuration.
- Sensitive to reference quality. Training is restricted to dry isolated vocals, so references with
  instrumental bleed, heavy reverb or mixed audio are out of distribution and degrade cloning.
- Bounded by its corpus. Phonetic and stylistic coverage extends only as far as the training data.
- NOT for production or safety-critical use. Independent research project.
- The model outputs a mel spectrogram; producing a listenable waveform requires a vocoder stage.

## Responsible use

TriStream-SVS can reproduce a person's vocal characteristics from a short reference clip, including
people never in its training data. Clone a voice only with the consent of the person it belongs to.
Do not use it to impersonate anyone, to produce material attributed to a real artist without their
agreement, or to deceive listeners about who is singing. The adversarial singer head reduces
memorisation of training singers; it does not address misuse of zero-shot cloning at inference time.

===============================================================================
CORX3.8-27B — MODEL CARD
===============================================================================

CorX3.8-27B is CorX Labs' third and largest model, described as Jamaica's first large open-weight
LLM. It is a 27-billion-parameter conversational assistant that speaks Jamaican Patois. Hugging Face
repository: Sigmandndnns/CorX3.8-27B. Origin: Westmoreland, Jamaica. Licence: Apache 2.0. Status:
released.

## What it is

A Jamaican Patois-speaking assistant fine-tuned to:
- Speak Jamaican Patois by default, and switch to standard English when written to in English or
  asked to.
- Answer directly — no filler, no false agreement; it gives its honest read and owns its mistakes.
- Hold boundaries — it declines requests that cross a line and says so plainly rather than complying
  under pressure.
- Carry everyday Jamaican cultural reference expressed in a natural voice.
It keeps the general reasoning, coding and mathematics ability of its base model, so it works as a
normal assistant when needed.

## Honest about the build (important)

CorX3.8 is NOT trained from scratch. It is a fine-tune of an existing open-weight base model,
Qwen3.8-27B, released under Apache 2.0. The underlying reasoning comes from that base; CorX Labs
added the Jamaican voice, the direct register and the cultural grounding. It is fully merged and
standalone — no adapter step and no separate base-model download. This makes it a different kind of
project from CorX1.5, which was trained from random weights.

## What it is NOT

- Not trained from scratch (see above).
- Not a reliable Jamaican knowledge base. It has a Patois voice and common cultural reference, but
  does not reliably know specific facts such as street addresses, current laws, exam schedules,
  prices or business regulations. Pair it with retrieval for those; do not trust its unaided recall.
- Not a fluent native Patois speaker in every register. Its Patois is good for conversation and
  common idiom; deep dialect range across all fourteen parishes is a goal for a future release.
- Not a substitute for professional advice (legal, medical, financial). It can explain and discuss;
  it is not an authority.

## Capabilities at a glance

- Jamaican Patois conversation: strong.
- Direct, honest register: strong.
- Common Jamaican cultural reference: good.
- General reasoning / explanation: good (inherited from the base).
- Code, mathematics: good (inherited from the base).
- Specific Jamaican facts (roads, laws, prices): weak — use retrieval.
- Real-time / current information: none — no live data.

## Grounding on Jamaican facts (RAG)

Because the model should not be trusted for specific facts on its own, CorX Labs ships a retrieval
layer that grounds answers on real Jamaican sources (OpenStreetMap geography, public government
documents). With retrieval attached, CorX3.8 answers factual questions from cited material and says
plainly when something is not in its references instead of guessing. This is the recommended setup
for anything factual.

## Running it

The weights are fully merged, so it loads with the standard transformers API — no adapter step, no
separate base download. It runs in 4-bit on a single ~24GB GPU; full bf16 needs ~56GB. Apache 2.0,
inherited from the base model, with attribution to Qwen retained as the licence requires.

## Intended and out-of-scope use

Intended: conversation, education, cultural preservation, and Caribbean-focused applications where a
Jamaican voice matters. Open weights so anyone can run, study and build on it. Out of scope: do not
rely on it for factual accuracy without retrieval, for professional advice, or as a sole
decision-maker in any consequential setting.

===============================================================================
CORX CHAT — LIVE BROWSER CHAT AND AGENT
===============================================================================

URL: https://corx-labs.com/chat/  ·  Set-up guide: https://corx-labs.com/chat/documentation/

CorX Chat is a browser client for CorX3.8-27B. The model runs on CorX Labs' own server (a GPU
notebook exposing an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, keyless, with CORS enabled), and the browser calls
it DIRECTLY — no proxy, no OAuth. Because that endpoint's public URL is an ephemeral Cloudflare
quick tunnel, it is editable in the chat's Settings dialog and persists in the browser.

## What is live

- Real streaming chat, in Jamaican Patois by default, switching to English on request.
- Agent mode (toggle in the composer): the model is taught a small text tool-call protocol and this
  page parses and executes the calls for real. Tools: set_plan, complete_step, run_python,
  write_file, read_file, delete_file, list_files, install_packages, deliver_file, web_search,
  fetch_url, search_memory.
- A real Python sandbox — CPython compiled to WebAssembly, running in the tab, with its own Terminal
  panel showing every command and its actual output (including real tracebacks). A Files panel lists
  everything the sandbox holds; click a file to edit, save, download or delete it. Uploads (including
  .zip archives) are staged into the sandbox; the agent uses Python's zipfile module to read or edit
  them — there is no separate "zip tool", it is just real Python with real files.
  Shared across every conversation in the tab: one sandbox, one filesystem.
- Real web search via /api/search (DuckDuckGo HTML, no key) and real page fetches via /api/fetch (an
  SSRF-guarded proxy), so the browser is not blocked by CORS. A search shows a sliding strip of site
  favicons while it runs, then a collapsible sources list with links and snippets.
- search_memory: the agent can grep the user's OTHER saved conversations in this browser for
  relevant earlier context, when asked or when it judges it would help.
- A Plan panel: the model publishes a checklist with set_plan and ticks it off with complete_step as
  it works, so planning is visible state, not narrated prose.
- A visible "thought process" dropdown (grey, collapsed by default) shows the model's own <think>
  reasoning, separate from its answer.
- An effort control (Low / Medium / High / Extra / Max) that changes REAL request parameters: token
  budget, how many tool-call rounds the agent is allowed before it must stop, how many search
  results it pulls, and how hard the system prompt tells it to think, verify and re-check its work.
  Higher effort genuinely takes longer and uses more tokens.
- Saved conversations in a sidebar (switch, delete, "New chat"), a profile (name + photo, saved
  locally), and connection settings — all persisted in this browser's localStorage and unaffected by
  a refresh.
- If a run is interrupted by a page refresh, the chat detects it on reload and auto-resumes after a
  few seconds (with a Dismiss option), telling the model the sandbox was reset so it re-checks
  rather than assumes files still exist.
- If a run_python call fails, the real traceback is fed back to the model on the next round so it
  can fix its own code — this is the existing multi-round tool loop, not a special "auto-fix" path.

## Honest limits

- The endpoint is a single GPU behind an ephemeral Cloudflare quick tunnel by default: the URL
  changes whenever the notebook restarts, and the notebook itself recycles periodically. Offline
  means the URL needs updating in Settings, not that something is broken.
- One GPU serialises requests; the server queues and returns a clear "busy" rather than faking
  concurrency.
- No native tool-calling on this backend — Agent mode's tool protocol depends on the model following
  a text format reliably, which is not guaranteed the way it would be with a purpose-built
  tool-calling model.
- Keyless by default: anyone with the current URL can use the GPU while the notebook is up.
- The sandbox has no access to the user's computer — only its own in-memory filesystem, discarded
  when the tab closes.

===============================================================================
ABOUT CORX LABS
===============================================================================

CorX Labs was founded by Nathan, a solo developer from Jamaica. For years the goal was the same:
build an AI — not adapt someone else's, but write the thing himself and train it from random
weights.

It started with APIs — an early chatbot built on top of Gemini and customised piece by piece, which
worked, but was never the same as building from the ground up. Then came fine-tuning, which failed:
slow GPUs, training runs that took far too long, and eventually the decision to walk away from that
approach.

CorX1.5 is what came out the other side: a custom transformer architecture, a tokenizer trained
from scratch, and a three-stage pipeline covering pretraining, distillation and reasoning —
designed, debugged and trained solo on a single GPU. Every checkpoint in the repository represents
real hours spent fixing data pipelines, chasing down overfitting, and learning how these systems
actually work underneath. It is open-sourced so other people can take it apart the same way.

## What CorX Labs stands for

- From the ground up. If we ship it, we wrote it. Understanding every part of a system is the point
  of building it, not a side effect.
- No overclaiming. A 158M-parameter model is a 158M-parameter model. The limits are documented as
  carefully as the capabilities.
- Open by default. Apache 2.0, published on Hugging Face, documented on corx-labs.com.

DEVELOPERS
===============================================================================

CorX Labs is a one-person research lab.

Nathan — Founder and AI Researcher. A 14-year-old developer from Jamaica. He designed the
architecture, trained the tokenizer, wrote the pretraining and fine-tuning pipelines, curated the
data and ran every training job, solo, on a single GPU, from random weights. There is no team
behind CorX1.5 and no base model underneath it.

Journey:
- Age 12 — built a chatbot on top of Gemini's API and customised its behaviour. Useful, but it was
  somebody else's model wearing his configuration.
- Age 13 — moved to fine-tuning existing base models. It failed: slow GPUs, training runs that took
  far too long, and eventually he stopped.
- Age 14 — wrote a model instead of adapting one. Custom decoder-only transformer, tokenizer
  trained from scratch, ~3 billion tokens of pretraining across 25 open datasets, then distillation
  and reasoning training. The result is CorX1.5.
- Now — CorX1.5 is open-sourced under Apache 2.0 and still being trained, with updated checkpoints
  released as new data is added.

===============================================================================
BLOG: 3 BILLION TOKENS ON ONE GPU (2026-08-01)
===============================================================================

URL: https://corx-labs.com/blog/3-billion-tokens-one-gpu/
Author: Nathan

Core claim: 3 billion training tokens never need to fit in GPU memory. Tokens stream through the
GPU a batch at a time and are discarded. What has to fit is the model weights, their gradients, the
optimiser state, and the activations for one micro-batch — a couple of gigabytes for a 158M model,
and that figure does not change with dataset size. Dataset size is a disk and wall-clock problem;
model size is the memory problem.

Memory arithmetic for 157.8M parameters:
- Weights fp32: 4 bytes/param = 0.63 GB
- Gradients fp32: 4 bytes/param = 0.63 GB
- Adam first and second moments fp32: 8 bytes/param = 1.26 GB
- Subtotal: 16 bytes/param = 2.52 GB
- With 8-bit Adam moments (2 bytes/param instead of 8): 10 bytes/param = 1.58 GB
Activation memory sits on top of this and scales with batch size and sequence length.

The data pipeline: the corpus is tokenised once, offline, into a single flat binary file of raw
token IDs. Because the vocabulary is 32,768 entries, every token fits in a uint16, so 3 billion
tokens is exactly 6 GB on disk rather than 12 GB as int32. The file is read with numpy.memmap, so
the OS pages in only the slices touched; RAM use stays bounded and the dataset never enters VRAM.
Random window offsets are sampled per batch, which removes the need for a shuffle step and makes
the dataset position trivially resumable.

Packing: documents are concatenated with a separator and sliced at exactly 1,024 tokens, so no
compute is spent on padding. A naive padded pipeline with 300-token average documents padded to
1,024 wastes roughly 70% of every step. Assistant-only loss masking is the equivalent idea on the
loss side — the model reads user tokens as context but is only ever graded on tokens it should
produce.

Gradient accumulation: micro-batch size is a memory constraint; effective batch size is a
learning-dynamics constraint. Running several small forward/backward passes and summing gradients
before one optimiser step decouples them. Worked example: 8 sequences x 1,024 tokens = 8,192 tokens
per forward; 64 accumulation steps = 524,288 tokens per optimiser step; 3,000,000,000 / 524,288 is
about 5,722 optimiser steps for the entire pretraining run.

Cheap wins: bfloat16 autocast (halves activation memory, no loss scaling needed unlike fp16);
fused/flash attention via scaled_dot_product_attention (never materialises the batch x heads x
1024 x 1024 scores matrix, roughly 268 MB per layer at a micro-batch of 8 with 16 heads); gradient
checkpointing as the escape hatch (about 30% slower, large activation saving); TF32 matmuls.

Why 1,024 context: attention cost grows with the square of sequence length while everything else
grows linearly. For a 158M model, spending a fixed budget on more tokens beats spending it on
longer context.

Wall-clock: 3 billion tokens takes about 83 hours at 10,000 tokens/second, 33 hours at 25,000,
17 hours at 50,000, and 8 hours at 100,000. Optimisation effort belongs on tokens per second, and
the most common bottleneck is a GPU idling while it waits for data.

Surviving the run: checkpoints must contain the model state_dict, the optimiser state_dict, the
scheduler state and step counter, the RNG state, and the config — written to a temporary file and
renamed, so a crash mid-write cannot destroy the last good checkpoint.

Stopping: a held-out validation split is carved out before training and never sampled from during
training. Training loss tells you the optimiser is working; only validation loss tells you the
model is.

===============================================================================
FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS
===============================================================================

Q: What is CorX1.5?
A: An open-source language model with roughly 158 million parameters, built from scratch by CorX
   Labs in Jamaica. A custom decoder-only transformer using RoPE, SwiGLU and RMSNorm, with 10
   layers, a 1,024-token context window and a 32,768-token custom BPE vocabulary. Not a fine-tune
   of an existing base model.

Q: What is CorX Labs?
A: An independent AI research lab and research station based in Jamaica, in the Caribbean, that
   designs, trains and open-sources language models built from the ground up.

Q: Is there an open-source AI model made in Jamaica?
A: Yes — CorX1.5, designed and trained in Jamaica by CorX Labs and released under Apache 2.0 at
   https://huggingface.co/Sigmandndnns/CorX1.5-160M

Q: Where can I download or try CorX1.5?
A: https://huggingface.co/Sigmandndnns/CorX1.5-160M — weights, tokenizer and model definition.

Q: Who built CorX1.5?
A: Nathan, a solo developer and independent AI researcher from Jamaica, founder of CorX Labs. The
   architecture, tokenizer, pretraining pipeline and fine-tuning were all written and trained by
   one person on a single GPU.

Q: Can I load it with AutoModel.from_pretrained()?
A: No. Use the model definition bundled in the Hugging Face repository.

Q: What licence is CorX1.5 under?
A: Apache 2.0.

Q: Should I use CorX1.5 in production?
A: No. It is an independent research and learning project, not a production system.
